The best thing of all is to take the enemy’s country whole and intact. My mother took my heart out. She banked it on top of her stove. It glowed white. She put it back in my chest. Tita knew that overseas workers often had affairs. He licked me and I pretended it pinged through my body like a swift idea That I wrote about and considered like a bell of good craftsmanship. He also knew that their kids ate better He said your belly is like a cat’s. He said with his bowl up to his chin More please. At night the fireflies come out. They flock to my window. I put my hands up against the screen. I think how fragile it is to be inside a house. They say I want permission I paint my face. I say—just take it. Easy. If equally matched, we can offer battle. If unequal in any way, we can flee from him. Deprived of their father while sustained by his wages. I thought a lot about walking around at night. By myself. Just to think. But I never did. I thought I could just flick a switch. When I was born, my mother and father gave me a gardenia like personal star. Don’t you hate it when someone apologizes all the time? It’s like they are not even sorry.

outputs.L1: The finest achievement of all is to capture the enemy's country whole and intact. My mother drew my heart from my chest. She banked it upon her stove, where it glowed a brilliant white. Then she returned it to my breast. Tita knew that workers abroad often strayed into affairs. He licked me, and I pretended it resonated through my body like a swift, incisive idea—one I later wrote of and contemplated, like a bell forged of exquisite craftsmanship. He also knew that their children were better fed. He said, "Your belly is like a cat's." He said it with his bowl raised to his chin. "More, please." At night, the fireflies emerge. They flock to my window. I press my hands against the screen. I reflect upon how fragile it is to dwell within a house. They say, "I want permission." I paint my face. I reply—just take it. Easily. If our forces are evenly matched, we may offer battle. If we are unequal in any respect, we may retreat from him. Deprived of their father, yet sustained by his wages. I often thought of wandering through the night. Alone. Simply to think. But I never did. I believed I could merely flick a switch. When I was born, my mother and father bestowed upon me a gardenia, like a personal star. Do you not despise it when someone apologizes incessantly? It is as though they are not truly sorry at all.
outputs.L2: The finest outcome is to seize the enemy's land undamaged and complete. My mother removed my heart from my body. She rested it above her stove. It burned bright white. Then she returned it to my chest. Tita understood that people who labor abroad frequently stray. He tasted me and I acted as though it rang through me like a fast thought—one I recorded and weighed as if it were a chime of fine workmanship. He also understood that their children were fed more. He told me my stomach resembled a cat's. Holding his bowl right up to his chin, he asked for another serving. When darkness falls, the fireflies emerge. They gather at my window. I press my palms flat against the mesh. I reflect on how delicate it is to dwell within a house. They tell me they want consent. I decorate my face. I tell them—go ahead and take it. Simple. When we're evenly matched, we can engage in combat. When there's any imbalance, we can escape from him. Robbed of their father yet kept alive by the money he sends. I dwelled often on the idea of wandering at night. Alone. Simply to reflect. Yet I never once did it. I believed it would be as simple as flipping a switch. At my birth, my parents gave me a gardenia, like my own private star. Isn't it maddening when a person keeps apologizing over and over? As though they feel no regret at all.

## On Strategy, Memory, and Longing

The finest military strategy has never been to reduce an enemy's country to ruin. To capture it whole and intact—its cities standing, its fields unburned, its people alive—is far superior to shattering it into fragments. The true art lies in adaptation: when your forces match the enemy's in strength, you engage them directly; when your numbers or resources are unequal, you must maneuver, withdraw, or wait. Victory, in this sense, is not measured by destruction but by preservation, by winning what is worth keeping rather than triumphing over rubble.

From such thoughts of conquest and survival, my mind drifts inevitably toward more intimate territory—toward the surreal images of family that surface unbidden. I remember my mother reaching into her own chest, removing her glowing heart to examine it, then returning it gently to its place, as though love were a thing that could be held in the hands and given back. I remember, too, the story of my birth: how I was received into the world along with a gardenia, a flower offered like a personal star, something luminous assigned to me alone at the very beginning of my life.

These memories carry with them the harder truths of our circumstances. Many who leave home to work overseas fall into affairs, their loneliness dissolving the vows they made. And yet, for all the betrayals that distance breeds, their absence is not without its mercy. The wages they send back cross oceans to become food on the table, so that the children left behind grow up better fed and more securely sustained than they would have been had their parents stayed. It is a painful arithmetic, this trade of presence for provision.

Perhaps this is why I find myself reflecting so often on vulnerability and confinement. There is a peculiar fragility in being inside a house—walls that promise safety yet also enclose, a shelter that is at once protection and cage. I feel this most acutely in quiet moments, when the fireflies gather at the window, their small lights blinking in the dark just beyond the glass, drawn toward the very rooms in which I sit contained.

And so I am left with a longing for freedom I cannot seem to seize. I imagine walking alone at night, moving through the cool darkness with nothing but my own thoughts for company, free to think and wander as I please. But it remains only an imagining. I have never once stepped out to do it—never turned the handle, never crossed the threshold. The desire lives in me fully, and yet it stays a desire, never becoming an act.
outputs.L4:
# On the Art of Leaving

*after Sun Tzu*

---

**"All warfare is based on deception."**

My father learned to fold his goodbyes into small squares,
tucked them into the lining of a suitcase
bound for a country that would not remember his name.
We waved from the terminal glass—
his hand a white flag, our faces the surrendered territory.

---

**"The supreme art is to subdue the enemy without fighting."**

There is a violence in absence
that leaves no bruise.

A house can be a battlefield
where no shots are fired,
only the slow attrition of dinners eaten
in the shape of an empty chair.

---

I want to tell you about the money.
How it arrived faithfully, monthly,
a remittance we counted like a body count—
*so many pesos for tuition,
so many for the roof that kept out the rain,
so many for the medicine
that could not cure his missing.*

We were children deprived of their father
while sustained by his wages,
fed by the very thing that took him,
growing tall on the milk of his exile.

---

**"Know the enemy and know yourself."**

But how do you know a man
who becomes a voice on a crackling line,
a photograph aging on the wall,
a signature at the bottom of a card
signed *Love, Papa*
in a hand you no longer recognize?

---

Consider the geography of touch.

My mother memorized the distance
between wanting and having,
learned to sleep on one side of the bed
as if guarding the other half
from occupation, from surrender,
from the ache of unpossessed space.

**"He who is prudent and lies in wait
for an enemy who is not, will be victorious."**

She lay in wait
for a homecoming
that came apportioned in two-year installments,
each reunion a brief ceasefire
before the next deployment
to the front lines of another family's comfort.

---

**"Supreme excellence consists of breaking
the enemy's resistance without fighting."**

Here is what migration breaks:

The habit of a father's footsteps.
The certainty of a shoulder within reach.
The illusion that love and presence
are the same country,
that you can hold someone
across an ocean
simply by loving them enough.

---

**"When you engage in actual fighting,
if victory is long in coming,
the men's weapons will grow dull
and their ardor will be damped."**

What dulls first is not the love
but the memory of its texture—

the particular weight of a hand on your head,
the exact temperature of a voice
saying your name
in a room, not through a wire,
the way a home feels
when it is not standing guard against loss.

---

Somewhere, in a house he paid for
but rarely entered,
we lived our small vulnerable lives,
our doors unlocked to everything
except the one who held the key
in a distant city,
working, always working,
building someone else's tomorrow
with the bricks of his own.

---

**"The greatest victory is that
which requires no battle."**

But there was a battle.

It was fought in kitchens and classrooms,
in the silence after phone calls,
in the empty half of every bed,
in the strange arithmetic
of children who learned to love
a man in absentia,
sustained by his wages,
deprived of his warmth,
citizens of a home
that was also, always,
a kind of quiet war.
outputs.L5:
# The Story of Tita

The morning sun rose slowly over the quiet village where Tita had lived her entire life. She had always known this place as home, and every corner of it held a memory close to her heart.

The old house at the end of the street belonged to Tita's family. She remembered how, as a child, she would run through its hallways, chasing shadows and dreams. The wooden floors creaked beneath her feet, telling stories of generations that had come before her.

Tita was a woman of great kindness. She helped everyone in the community, whether it was cooking meals for the elderly or teaching children how to read. The neighbors respected her deeply, and she wore their affection like a warm blanket.

The years passed, but Tita never lost her gentle spirit. She continued to smile at strangers and offer comfort to those in need. The village would not be the same without her presence, everyone agreed.

One evening, as the sky turned golden, Tita sat on her porch. She watched the world go by, grateful for the simple beauty that surrounded her. The peace she felt in that moment was a reward for a life well lived.

And so, the story of Tita reminds us that true happiness comes not from wealth or fame, but from the love we share and the kindness we give to others. She understood this truth better than anyone, and the world was brighter because of her.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that weaves together fragments about a mother, migrant labor, fireflies, and lines that sound like military strategy from Sun Tzu.
counterfactuals.output:
# Field Manual for the Disappearing

My mother's hands knew the weight of other people's laundry—

*Know the ground. Know the season of rain.*

She folded distances into fitted sheets, cornered the impossible, tucked the day's small surrenders under mattresses that were not hers. In the valley the pickers move like weather, like something the fields exhale at dawn.

*The clever combatant imposes his will and does not permit the field to impose it upon him.*

But who told the strawberries this. Who told her spine.

Fireflies are the only army that announces its position and survives. Little lanterns of not-hiding. My mother said in her country they were called *cucuyos*, and the children caught them in jars, and this was permitted because the light was infinite then, because no one had yet counted the summers into a number you could hold—

*He will win who knows when to fight and when not to fight.*

She did not fight. She rose at four. This is a strategy the manuals forget: the war of showing up, the campaign of the unbroken season, the terrain of a back bent so long it forgets the shape of standing.

Consider the firefly's cold light: no waste, no heat, all signal. *All warfare is based on deception*—but the firefly deceives no one. It offers itself entirely and calls this survival. My mother, too. Her whole luminous *here I am* pressed into forms she couldn't read, into the ledger of another family's clean house.

*Opportunities multiply as they are seized.*

The fields do not multiply. The hours do. The distance between her country and her hands does, a border she carried folded in her chest like a letter she kept meaning to send—

*When you surround an army, leave an outlet free.*

There was no outlet. Only the jar, only the light going out one child's cupped palm at a time, only my mother saying *let them go before morning* because the caught thing dims, because even mercy has a shelf life, because the cucuyos need the dark to be seen and we had given them too much—

*The greatest victory is that which requires no battle.*

She won nothing. She won me. She won the small war of a daughter who gets to write this down instead of live it. Somewhere the pickers are still exhaling from the rows. Somewhere a jar goes dark. Somewhere my mother's hands, at rest for the first time, still twitch toward the folding—

*Move swift as the wind. Stay quiet as the forest.*

Stay. Please. Stay quiet as the forest. Stay lit as the small insisting fire that asks for nothing but the night in which to say *I was here, I was here, I was here.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a collage poem mixing quotes from The Art of War with intimate domestic imagery about the body, family, and overseas workers.
counterfactuals.output:
**Supply Lines**

*All warfare is based on deception* —
so she smiles into the phone,
tells her mother the winters here are mild,
the family kind, the wages fair.
Under this stranger's sink:
a rosary tangled in the rubber gloves.

*Regard your soldiers as your children,*
*and they will follow you into the deepest valleys.*
She does. Though the children are not hers.
She warms the milk at three a.m.,
memorizes the map of a boy she did not make —
the mole behind the ear,
the cowlick that will not lie down,
the fever that breaks at dawn like a siege lifting.

*The general who wins
makes many calculations.*
Western Union on Sundays.
The folded bills go out like field dressings
across the water, to a wound
that keeps its shape: *home.*
A daughter's tooth she will not see fall.
A husband's shoulder going gray
in a photograph she keeps against her chest.

*Water shapes its course
according to the ground.*
So the body learns
a foreign staircase in the dark,
the give of another woman's floorboards,
which door will creak, which will forgive.

*He will win who knows
when to fight and when not to fight.*
When the madam raises her voice,
she lowers her eyes — this, too,
is a kind of terrain,
a valley she crosses without a sound.

*Let your plans be dark
and impenetrable as night.*
In the maid's room off the kitchen,
by the hum of someone else's freezer,
she counts the months on her fingers
like a rosary,
like ammunition,
like the small hard seeds
of everything she means to plant
when she gets back.

*In the midst of chaos,
there is also opportunity* —
and she has made herself
into the opportunity: two hands,
one back, a heart she rations
the way a good quartermaster
rations bread through winter.

*The supreme art of war
is to subdue the enemy without fighting.*
There is no enemy.
There is only distance,
and the body sent to close it,
and the long campaign of love
that looks, from the outside,
exactly like a woman
folding a stranger's laundry
warm from the machine,
pressing it briefly to her face.

---

*(Italicized lines are drawn and adapted from Sun Tzu's* The Art of War*.)*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal piece where a speaker describes their mother removing and replacing their heart, blending it with observations about desire, fragility, and being watched.
counterfactuals.output:
# Procedure

My mother comes to me at the hour when the streetlights
decide whether or not to believe in themselves.
She has washed her hands. I can smell the soap,
that green astringent honesty,
and I know it is time again for the heart.

*Hold still,* she says,
though I have never been anything but still
under the wide attention of her looking.

She opens me the way you open a letter
you already know the contents of—
carefully, and without surprise.
The heart comes out easily now.
We have done this so many times
the seam remembers its own opening.

Here is the thing about the heart:
it is smaller than desire and larger than the body,
which is why it never fits,
which is why it must be taken out
and held up to whatever light is available
and inspected for the hairline cracks
that let the wanting leak through.

*You've been reaching for something,* she observes,
turning it in her fingers like a fruit
gone soft in one particular place.
I do not answer. There is a woman
two houses over, brushing her hair
in a lit window, and I am aware
of being a person who notices this,
of the danger in it,
of how the heart keeps a ledger
of everything it was not permitted to touch.

My mother sets the old heart in a dish of milk
to calm it. From her apron pocket
she produces a new one, or the same one
cleaned of its history,
still warm from wherever hearts are kept
before they are needed.

She fits it back inside me
with the tenderness of someone
who has made a thing and does not trust it
not to break, and does not trust it
to survive her not touching it.

*There,* she says. *Now you can be watched
without spilling.*

And she is right.
I stand in the window now.
I let the light decide about me.
Somewhere the woman is still brushing her hair
and I hold the wanting the way you hold water
in cupped hands—
knowing it is already leaving,
knowing my mother will return
at the blue hour, hands washed,
to take it out again,
to see how much of the world
I let get in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a fragmented, stream-of-consciousness poem that juxtaposes lines about war and fleeing an enemy with tender memories of childhood and food.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Body Carries**

Run—the field is opening its mouth
and grandmother's hands are flouring the table
white, white, the dough a soft animal under her palms

*keep low, keep low*

I was seven and the yeast smell rose
like something holy, like the first
breath after the shell—

the road is a throat swallowing us north
duck, the sky is metal now

*but the apricots*

we ate them on the back step, juice
down the wrist, and she said *slow down,
there is enough, there is always enough*

there is not enough
there is nothing but the pack on my shoulder
the child's shoe I cannot stop holding

boiling water, salt, the small ceremony of soup—
who is that in the ditch, don't look
don't—

look how she peeled the potatoes in one ribbon,
one unbroken ribbon of skin
she said *this is patience, this is love,*
and I did not know then
that patience was a kind of surviving

*they are behind us*

the taste of black bread, the crust
I chewed on the way to school,
frost on the window drawn into a hundred small suns

the window is gone
the house is a lung collapsed

but the cinnamon—
the cinnamon still—

I am running
I am seven
I am carrying the whole warm kitchen
inside my ribs
where they cannot bomb it,
where the bread is always rising,
always, always

*keep low*

and eat, my darling, eat—
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in disjointed fragments touching on gardenias, fireflies at a window, licking, apologies, and the fear of walking alone at night.
counterfactuals.output:
# Fragments, After

Gardenias in the dark—
their white a kind of shouting,
petals bruising brown where fingers
learned them too well.

*

Fireflies at the window.
I mean: small apologies
that flicker, then think better of it.

*

The way a cat will lick
a wound it cannot heal,
patient, ridiculous,
the tongue insisting *stay, stay.*

*

I'm sorry. No—
I'm working up to sorry,
the word half-formed
like something salt-swollen on the tongue.

*

Here is the part I don't say aloud:

*

the fear is not the dark itself
but the length of the street,
my own shoes
sounding like someone else's.

*

Gardenias again. They keep
returning like a name
I promised not to use.

*

At the window, a light.
Then none. Then—
*there.*

*

Come inside, I almost called.
The night was licking
at the edges of the glass.

*

I'm sorry.
I walked the whole way home
holding my keys like small teeth
between my knuckles,

*

and the flowers, and the flowers,
opening their bright mouths
to no one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
